papers.title: Extracellular Lactate Inhibits HIV Infection in Dendritic Cells by Downregulating CD4 Expression
papers.abstract: Cellular metabolism and cellular microenvironments influences immune-cell function. We previously demonstrated that interleukin-27 (IL-27)-induced monocyte-derived dendritic cells (27DCs) exhibit resistance to HIV-1. A mechanistic study for this antiviral effect suggested that in addition to inducing antiviral genes, IL-27 may influence cellular metabolism that contributes to the anti-HIV effect. During course of study, we observed that 27DCs accumulated lactate in culture supernatants by 5.7-fold increase compared with cultures of untreated DCs (iDCs) (12.1{+/-}1.3 versus 2.1{+/-}0.2 mM). Here, we assesses extracellular role of lactate on HIV infection. Healthy donors CD14+ monocytes were differentiated to DCs using GM-CSF and IL-4 in the absence of presence of lactate (Lac). DCs were infected with HIVAD8. Lactate-induced DC (LacDC) reduced R5-tropic HIV-1 AD8 replication by 71.1{+/-}8.3% without detectable cytotoxicity compared to that in untreated cells (iDCs). LacDCs exhibited reductions in viral particles binding, membrane fusion of viral particles, and HIV reverse-transcription by 78.5{+/-}2.8% (n=3, p<0.05), 78.7{+/-}3.3% (n=3, p<0.01), 86.2{+/-}5.7% (n=3. p<0.01), respectively. FACS analyses demonstrated that surface CD4 expression on LacDC decreased by 56.6{+/-}5.1% (n=5 , p<0.05) compared to iDC, whereas total cellular CD4 protein amount and surface CCR5 expression were not significantly altered. Neither the lactate transporter inhibitor nor the lactate receptor restored HIV-1 susceptibility. These findings demonstrate that lactate exposure during dendritic-cell differentiation induces an HIV-1-resistant phenotype associated with reduced surface CD4 availability and impaired viral attachment. This study identifies extracellular lactate as a modulator of dendritic-cell susceptibility to HIV-1 and suggests a potential link between IL-27-associated metabolic changes and antiviral immunity.

papers.title: Extensive SARS-CoV-2 spike sequence diversification converges on a bounded, low-dimensional physicochemical space
papers.abstract: During the COVID-19 pandemic, SARS-CoV-2 accumulated extensive amino acid variation in its spike protein. However, the extent to which sequence diversification translates into physicochemical diversity remains unclear. Here, we analyzed 271,769 unique spike protein sequences from 12 geographical regions using three physicochemical descriptors: net charge at pH 7.0, hydropathy, and aliphatic index. To characterize temporal changes in physicochemical space, we compared the squared Mahalanobis distances of observed sequences with those of Monte Carlo-simulated sequences containing randomized amino acid substitutions, constrained to the number of empirically variable positions. We applied trimmed clustering to characterize sequence distributions in physicochemical space and used Shannon entropy to assess spatiotemporal relationships between genotypic and physicochemical diversity across geographic regions. Empirical physicochemical displacement increased early in the observation period and subsequently stabilized, despite continued increases in variable amino acid positions and accumulated substitutions. In contrast, simulated trajectories exhibited greater and sustained physicochemical divergence. Trimmed clustering identified six distinct physicochemical groups repeatedly occupied by genetically divergent lineages differing in mutation burden, amino acid composition, and emergence time. Shannon entropy analyses revealed broadly similar nonlinear temporal patterns across geographic regions, with differences between genotypic and physicochemical entropy tending to be negative. These findings indicate that extensive spike protein sequence diversification occurred within a comparatively restricted physicochemical space, consistent with a many-to-one relationship between amino acid sequences and physicochemical states. This framework provides a quantitative approach for investigating physicochemical constraints on viral protein evolution and may inform future machine learning approaches to epitope prediction and vaccine antigen design.

papers.title: Mapping the genetic landscape of cell morphogenesis and subcellular organization in stationary-phase Escherichia coli cells
papers.abstract: In nature, many bacteria reside in a non-growing stationary phase. The extent and genetic basis of the accompanying cellular remodeling remain unclear. Here, we developed Coli-Painting, a combinatorial staining assay, and BactoScoop, a dedicated image-based profiling pipeline, to characterize the growth-to-stasis transition in Escherichia coli. Single-cell profiles revealed a gradual yet heterogeneous entry, with some cells retaining signs of chromosome replication or cell division well into stationary phase. Subsequent genome-wide profiling identified genetic determinants of stationary-phase cell morphology, nucleoid organization, RNA distribution, and membrane-related properties. Global correlations among cellular features revealed coordinated aspects of stationary-phase cell architecture, while high-dimensional mutant profiles provided functional context for genes of known and unknown function. Downstream characterization of 19 y-genes highlighted the ability of our approach to identify relevant contributors to stationary-phase physiology. Overall, our work uncovers the genetic landscape of stationary-phase cell organization in E. coli and serves as a resource for uncovering growth-stage-specific gene function.

papers.title: An HWE/HisKA2-family kinase-phosphatase pair differentially regulates two paralogous PhyR response regulators to shape the General Stress Response specificity in Sphingopyxis granuli TFA
papers.abstract: The general stress response (GSR) enables bacteria to withstand diverse environmental challenges. In Alphaproteobacteria, the GSR is controlled by a partner-switching mechanism involving the extracytoplasmic function sigma factor EcfG, its anti-sigma factor NepR, and the response regulator PhyR. Phosphorylated PhyR binds to NepR, releasing EcfG to activate GSR gene expression. However, how upstream signalling coordinates multiple PhyR paralogs remains poorly understood. Sphingopyxis granuli TFA is a pollutant-degrading bacterium able to use the organic solvent tetralin as a sole carbon and energy source. TFA contains two copies of each core GSR regulatory component, including two PhyR paralogs with distinct contributions to GSR activity and stress resistance. Using genetic, physiological and biochemical approaches, we identify two HWE/HisKA2-family proteins, HK_3483 and HK_1165, as major positive and negative GSR regulators, respectively. HK_3483 functions as a histidine kinase required for effective GSR activation through either PhyR paralog and for resistance to oxidative stress, copper and desiccation. It directly phosphorylates both PhyR proteins in vitro, with a preference for PhyR1. In contrast, HK_1165 preferentially dephosphorylates PhyR2. Consistently, deletion of SGRAN_1165 in a {Delta}phyR1 background increases PhyR2 phosphorylation in vivo under oxidative stress and stationary phase. Loss of HK_1165 causes a pronounced growth defect that is suppressed by deletion of either PhyR paralog while the remaining PhyR paralog supports elevated GSR activity and broad stress resistance. Our findings support a model in which differential regulation of PhyR phosphorylation, mediated by the opposing activities of an upstream kinase-phosphatase pair, contributes to functional specialization within bacterial stress signalling networks.

papers.title: Dog shelter facilitated transmission and maintenance of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in canine hookworms
papers.abstract: Anthelmintic resistance in canine hookworms is increasingly recognised; however, environmental settings that maintain and disseminate resistance-associated alleles remain poorly defined. We hypothesised that urban dog shelters act as hotspots for transmission of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in Ancylostoma caninum. Residual faecal samples (n=173) were collected from a Sydney, Australia metropolitan shelter over four sampling periods and analysed using coprodiagnostic methods and deep amplicon sequencing targeting ITS-2 and isotype-1 {beta}-tubulin loci. Hookworm eggs were detected in 41% of samples, with A. caninum identified in 97% of sequenced infections and U. stenocephala in 8%. The isotype-1 {beta}-tubulin F167Y mutation was detected in 83% of A. caninum-positive samples, although high allele frequencies (>70%) were uncommon. Longitudinal sampling identified ten dogs that acquired A. caninum during shelter residence, nine of which acquired populations carrying the F167Y mutation. These findings support the role of dog shelters as hotspots for maintenance and dissemination of benzimidazole resistance-associated alleles in canine hookworms. While the impact of this dissemination remains uncertain, ongoing surveillance and targeted anthelmintic stewardship are likely to be important in high-density dog populations.

papers.title: Conjugative delivery of a miniature Cas nuclease for broad range recipient gene editing
papers.abstract: Efficient delivery of the Cas endonuclease into target cells avoiding toxic effects remains one of the limiting steps of CRISPR-Cas gene editing technologies. Bacterial conjugation delivers protein and DNA directly into recipient bacteria, since the conjugative relaxase travels through a type IV secretion system covalently attached to the transferred DNA strand. We previously showed that fusion proteins relaxase- Cas12a or relaxase- base editor are translocated by conjugation and recover gRNA-guided nuclease or base-editing activity in recipient bacteria, despite the large size of the fusion. Aiming to improve the efficiency and to broaden the range of susceptible recipient bacteria, here we test translocation of the miniature type V-U4 nuclease Cas12n, fused to two unrelated conjugative relaxases, MobA and TrwC from RSF1010 and R388 respectively. Both fusions of 139 and 168 kDa were stably produced in Escherichia coli donor cells, mobilized their cognate plasmid as efficiently as the wild-type relaxases, and directed guide-dependent cleavage of a chromosomal target in the donor. Translocation and activity in recipient cells were tested with a lethality assay based on the loss of transconjugants viability caused by double-strand breaks introduced by the translocated nuclease. When MobA-Cas12n was delivered together with a mobilizable plasmid which encoded the guide RNA, conjugation frequency was reduced by more than one order of magnitude relative to both a non-targeting guide RNA and a nuclease-free relaxase control, indicating target-specific cleavage of the recipient chromosome. When assayed in parallel with previously characterized TrwC-Cas12a, MobA-Cas12n showed better protein yields and higher activity in recipient cells. This work extends the range of Cas proteins deliverable by conjugative relaxases to miniature nucleases. The fusion with relaxase MobA allows the use of the promiscuous RP4 conjugative system for conjugative delivery, extending the range of recipient bacteria potentially targeted by this tool.

papers.title: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analysis of oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid against extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing Escherichia coli in an in vitro bladder infection model: impact on clinical breakpoints
papers.abstract: Uropathogens with acquired ESBL-genes can limit effective oral treatment options. Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid can be used as targeted therapy (500/125mg, 8-hourly). Despite favorable urinary pharmacokinetics (PK), there is little urine-specific data that quantifies the exposure required for bacterial clearance. A dynamic in vitro bladder model was employed, allowing for the simulated treatment of UTIs with oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid. Sixteen Escherichia coli isolates (12 clinical ceftriaxone-resistant uropathogens, 4 laboratory isolates) were selected. Bacterial response to treatment, emergence of resistance, exposure-response targets and PK/PD indexes were explored. Following simulation of standard-dose oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid (500/125mg, 8-hourly; Cmax 935mg/L; AUC0-24 14272mg/L), 14/16 isolates displayed no growth at the end of treatment, with elimination in seven isolates confirmed after a 24h antibiotic-free follow up. As exposure was reduced, greater survival and regrowth were observed. Only two isolates had significant post-exposure rises in MIC (32 to 128mg/L, 64 to 256mg/L). %T>MIC was the best predictor for end of treatment outcome (?log10cfu/mL: stasis 52.7%, 1log10 kill 61.8%, 2log10 kill 71.1%, R2=0.9062). Lower R2 values were found with EUCAST MIC measurements (fixed 2mg/L clavulanic acid) as compared to CLSI MIC measurements (2:1 amoxicillin to clavulanic acid). Monte Carlo simulations indicated that standard-dose 8-hourly would achieve all %T>MIC targets in >95% of virtual patients with MICs ?64 mg/L, regardless of MIC method (CLSI or EUCAST). Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid displays time-dependent killing against ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli. This data supports clinical breakpoints for uncomplicated UTI for isolates with MIC ? 64mg/L, assuming 500/125mg oral dosing 8-hourly.

papers.title: Transfer learning for identification of filamentous fungi using culture and microscopy images.
papers.abstract: Culture morphology and microscopy images are required for identification of moulds. Automated image classification is achievable in specific domains via transfer learning of pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The study aimed to evaluate the classification accuracy of ResNet50 CNN, for image-based classification of seven commonly isolated filamentous fungi. A total of 15,400 images were collected from seven filamentous fungi. For each species, 1,100 images each were collected for two image modalities: culture front, and microscopy, resulting in 2,200 images per class. Images from each modality for each fungus, were divided into training, validation, and test sets. The ResNet-50 model was trained and validated using four approaches: culture images (n=7,000), microscopy images (n=7,000), ensemble approach incorporating both culture and microscopy images (n=14,000), and combined culture and microscopy grid images (n=7,000). Performance was evaluated using the independent test dataset comprising images from previously unseen fungal strains, which included 700 images each, for culture, microscopy and grid images, and 1,400 images for assessment of ensemble training approach. We applied transfer learning, using both ResNet50 with and without a hierarchical approach, and evaluated their performance on the test image sets. The highest classification accuracy was achieved using the culture and grid image models, both of which achieved overall accuracy of 100%. The microscopy only and ensemble models achieved overall accuracies of 99.4% and 98.8%, respectively.

papers.title: In vitro reduction of mineral oil hydrocarbons by Lacticaseibacillus casei DSM 20011
papers.abstract: Mineral oil hydrocarbons (MOH) are food contaminants of increasing concern due to their widespread occurrence in food and potential health risks. Although various physicochemical and biological strategies have been investigated to reduce chemical contaminants in food, the ability of lactic acid bacteria (LAB) to remove MOH has not previously been explored. The present study aimed to evaluate the in vitro removal of MOH by Lacticaseibacillus casei DSM 20011 under incubation 0for 4 h with shaking at 100 rpm. Following the screening of different LAB strains, L. casei DSM 20011 was selected for in vitro evaluation of MOH removal using a representative mineral oil mixture, followed by the determination of MOH by on-line LC GC-FID. L. casei DSM 20011 reduced MOH concentrations by up to approximately 80% (p < 0.05), with comparable reductions observed for the MOSH and MOAH fractions and no clear evidence of preferential removal of either fraction. Cell wall adsorption has been proposed as a mechanism contributing to PAH removal by LAB. Given the structural similarity between PAH and the MOAH fraction of MOH, together with the lack of recognized hydrocarbon-degrading enzymes in LAB, adsorption to the bacterial cell wall may also explain the observed MOH removal, although this hypothesis requires experimental confirmation. These findings identify the food-derived L. casei DSM 20011 as a promising candidate for the biological reduction of MOH contamination and provide a foundation for future studies investigating the mechanisms underlying MOH removal and validating its effectiveness in complex food matrices.

papers.title: Long-term Epstein-Barr virus persistence in immunocompetent, primate-related Chinese tree shrews and inducible lytic reactivation in species-matched epithelial cultures
papers.abstract: Experimental models combining long-term Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection in immunocompetent animals with species-matched cellular systems for studying viral regulation remain limited. Chinese tree shrews combine evolutionary proximity to primates with small-animal practicality and native immunocompetence, offering a complementary nonrodent model. We serially monitored blood and oral specimens from six animals inoculated with Akata EBV. Five were followed for approximately two years, including two beyond two years, and the sixth underwent tissue collection at approximately six months. Intermittent EBV DNA detection included blood positivity beyond two years in one animal. Viral RNA localized to liver, lung, and spleen at six months and to liver and spleen of another animal near two years, supporting persistent infection. All tested blood and oral specimens from six uninoculated controls were negative. In parallel, renewable lung-derived epithelial/mesothelial-like cultures maintained EBV infection in two immortalization backgrounds. Viral profiling identified Qp-associated EBNA1 transcription and latency-associated expression alongside spontaneous lytic transcription. Host transcriptomics identified 684 robust EBV-associated expression changes, with prominent enrichment of MYC and E2F target programs and metabolic pathways, together with reduced interferon- and inflammatory-response transcription across both backgrounds. These findings nominate MYC/E2F-associated host programs as candidate regulators of the balance between maintained infection and lytic activity. Zta expression and sodium butyrate induced lytic reactivation, with infectious virus production demonstrated after sodium butyrate treatment. This integrated platform complements humanized mice and nonhuman-primate models and connects long-term EBV persistence in vivo with experimentally accessible studies of host regulation and the latent-to-lytic transition in species-matched cultures.

papers.title: Computational identification and in vitro evaluation of astragaloside II as an inhibitor of dengue virus NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability
papers.abstract: Background Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral disease in which severe cases are marked by leakage of plasma from blood vessels. The secreted nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) of dengue virus damages the endothelial barrier and is a drug target, but no approved antiviral exists. We aimed to identify compounds that target NS1 and to test whether the selected compound, astragaloside II (ASII), counteracts NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability. Methodology/Principal findings We built a deep learning model that predicts compound-target binding from chemical fingerprints and protein sequences, and used it to prescreen 177 natural compounds against NS1 of the four dengue virus serotypes. The model outperformed the DeepConv-DTI baseline in recall and F1-score on a BindingDB holdout set and on two independent test sets. ASII was predicted to bind NS1 and was docked onto the NS1 dimer. In human microvascular endothelial cells (HMEC-1), NS1 reduced the relative trans-endothelial electrical resistance to 0.56 (P < 0.001), whereas ASII at 10-30 {micro}g/mL kept resistance close to control levels without detectable cytotoxicity. ASII did not reduce NS1 internalization. In a competitive enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, ASII inhibited NS1 binding to heparan sulfate in a dose-dependent manner (half-maximal inhibitory concentration 51.12 {micro}g/mL; 95% confidence interval 47.91-56.24 {micro}g/mL), although inhibition at the protective doses was only 8-26%. Conclusions/Significance ASII is a candidate for further study as a modulator of NS1-induced endothelial hyperpermeability. Its mechanism remains unresolved and requires further study. Direct binding to NS1, activity in infected cells and effects in other endothelial models were not tested here, and the computational predictions require experimental confirmation.

papers.title: High-Throughput Screen of Advanced Repurposing Library Identifies Compounds Active Against Acute and Chronic Stages of Toxoplasma gondii
papers.abstract: Toxoplasma gondii, a pathogen with a global burden impacting millions, has the capability to interconvert between the actively replicating tachyzoite form into a semidormant bradyzoite for, complicating treatment. Here, we utilized an advanced high throughput screen (HTS) to identify repurposing candidates from the ReFRAME library, which consolidates 14,095 molecules from three major databases, including FDA approved and late-stage clinical leads. To facilitate screening, the permissive cyst-forming Tg68 strain was genetically engineered to express nano luciferase under the pBAG1 promoter to track bradyzoite growth, and firefly luciferase under the pTub1 promoter to monitor tachyzoite growth. HTS in 384 well format identified 160 compounds that exhibited > 80% inhibition at 10 micromolar of both tachyzoites and bradyzoites. By cross referencing against a publicly available HEK293T cytotoxicity dataset, we filtered out 61 compounds based on half-maximal cytotoxicity (CC50) less 20) against HepG2. The top hits were profiled using in vitro growth assays for tachyzoites, bradyzoites, and ex vivo liberated and intact cysts. Marizomib, monensin, narasin, and LY2090314 showed the strongest inhibition following 24 h treatment of intact cysts. When tested in combination with clinical compounds atovaquone and pyrimethamine, the top hits were predominantly additive. Additionally, they were evaluated for their potential for developing resistance using a minimum inoculum of resistance (MIR) assay. Six of nine compounds tested in MIR assays yielded no detectable parasites over 30 days. In contrast, LY2090314 resistant populations exhibited 26 to 29-fold resistance and carried a TgGSK3 L53V mutation, identifying a candidate resistance determinant. Collectively, our findings identify compounds with activity against tachyzoites and bradyzoites and with low propensity for resistance, as starting points for mechanistic investigation and further evaluation of in vivo efficacy and host-toxicity liabilities.

papers.title: Optimizing Avian Influenza Viral RNA Enrichment from Water: A Comparison of Concentration Methods for Low-Volume Samples
papers.abstract: Feed-baited water bins may provide a complementary approach for avian influenza virus (AIV) surveillance in wild waterbird populations. In a previous study, water from these bins was sampled using swabs after exposure to visiting birds, but the low sample volume limited the detection and subsequent characterization of AIV RNA (F. I. Rondi, J. Neumann-Heise, T. Harder, V. Allendorf, K. Depner, T. Homeier-Bachmann, L. Breuer, S. Knauf, S. Dreyer, and A. Globig, One Health 23:101548, 2026, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.onehlt.2026.101548). Here, we compared five sample-processing methods for improving AIV RNA detection in small (40-mL) water samples (tap and brackish water) spiked with an AIV of the H4N6 subtype under simulated field conditions: swab sampling, polyethylene glycol precipitation, activated carbon capture, combined activated carbon capture and polyethylene glycol precipitation (AC/PEG), and electronegative membrane adsorption (EM). AC/PEG and EM showed the strongest overall performance based on RT-qPCR results, although their relative performance varied across experimental conditions. The qPCR-derived viral signal was generally higher in tap water than in brackish water, whereas wheat presence was associated with a lower signal, particularly for swab sampling. Subsequent testing was conducted to ascertain the most effective storage conditions with regard to temperature and duration. During storage, AIV RNA detection remained relatively stable at minus 20 degrees Celsius for up to four weeks, with only minor increases in mean Ct values in both water matrices. Greater increases were observed at room temperature and 4 degrees Celsius, with significantly higher Ct values at both temperatures than at minus 20 degrees Celsius in both water matrices at Weeks 2 and 4 (p < 0.05). These findings support the potential of AC/PEG and EM to facilitate the recovery, detection and subsequent characterization of AIV from low-volume water samples by improving viral RNA detection using RT-qPCR. Given its overall performance and lower cost compared with EM, AC/PEG may represent a practical option for field-based surveillance. Regarding storage, minus 20 degrees Celsius provided the best conditions for maintaining AIV RNA detection, with relatively stable results for up to four weeks.

papers.title: Gain-of-function mutations in 1-phosphofructokinase (FruK) re-establish glycolysis in bacteria
papers.abstract: Secondary (promiscuous) activities provide enzymes with a reservoir of latent catalytic functions, which can be leveraged during selective pressure. Here we retrace the re-emergence of glycolysis from the promiscuous activity of 1-phosphofructokinase (FruK). We evolved a hexose-degradation-deficient Escherichia coli strain on glucose and recovered non-synonymous mutations in fruK. Reverse engineering, gene deletions and transcript quantification identified a modified and strongly overexpressed fruK as the determinant of the growth phenotype. Purified FruK variants phosphorylated fructose-6-phosphate in vitro, the best variant with ~170-fold improved catalytic efficiency over the wildtype enzyme. Crystal structures at up to 1.4 angstrom resolution captured FruK with ADP and either F1P, F6P or FBP bound. They identify a single active-site lysine that excludes the alternative substrate, and which E. coli FruK retains despite forgoing a 26 % gain in efficiency on its own native reaction. Since F1P, the product of the reverse reaction of FruK, is the effector of the global regulator Cra, we propose that this residue keeps glycolytic flux separate from transcriptional control. The same active-site motifs occur naturally across FruK clades, and a hexose-degradation-deficient Corynebacterium glutamicum strain converged on the same adaptation, indicating a common strategy across the Gram divide. The committed step of EMP glycolysis therefore lies a single substitution away within a widespread sugar kinase family, where it appears to be actively suppressed.

papers.title: Diabetes-associated lung physiology shapes Klebsiella pneumoniae infection dynamics
papers.abstract: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with increased susceptibility to bacterial pneumonia, yet the mechanisms by which diabetic host physiology influences pathogen establishment remain incompletely understood. Here, we investigated how diabetes-associated changes in the lung environment influence Klebsiella pneumoniae infection using leptin receptor-deficient (db/db) mice. Following acute lung infection, db/db mice exhibited increased bacterial burdens compared to nondiabetic controls, despite mounting a robust inflammatory cytokine response. Elevated pulmonary vascular endothelial growth factor concentrations were accompanied by alterations in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metabolite profile, including enrichment of several amino acids and related metabolites. Consistent with increased nutrient availability, K. pneumoniae exhibited enhanced growth in BALF from db/db mice, and a glutamate-auxotrophic mutant demonstrated improved fitness during pulmonary infection. Using a barcoded K. pneumoniae library, we found that db/db mice supported significantly larger initial founding populations, leading to increased bacterial burden in the lungs. Increased founding populations were also observed in the liver and coincided with proportionally wider infection bottlenecks in the lung. Together, these findings demonstrate that diabetes-associated changes in lung physiology coincide with increased nutrient availability and reduced restrictions on bacterial establishment, highlighting bacterial founding population size as a distinct determinant of pneumonia susceptibility in T2DM.

papers.title: H9N2 avian influenza virus in Bangladesh: three genetically distinct co-circulating subgroups retain a largely conserved antigenic phenotype
papers.abstract: Low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) H9N2 viruses are endemic in poultry across Bangladesh, causing substantial economic losses and posing a persistent zoonotic risk. Although genetic surveillance has documented ongoing viral evolution, the relationship between genetic diversification and antigenic change remains poorly understood. This study investigated the genetic diversity, reassortment, and antigenic characteristics of contemporary H9N2 viruses circulating in Bangladesh. Phylogenetic analysis of 219 sampled sequences revealed three genetically distinct monophyletic haemagglutinin (HA) G-lineage sub-groups, each characterised by unique amino acid substitutions. In contrast, neuraminidase (NA) displayed similar genetic diversity without distinct phylogenetic clusters. A dual-metric analysis of paired HA and NA phylogenies identified 20 putative reassortant H9N2 viruses. Further analysis showed that genetic diversity was geographically structured; however, all three HA subgroups co-circulated across multiple regions, and some live bird markets contained representatives of all three groups simultaneously, suggesting that live bird markets may facilitate mixing between genetically distinct viruses, and create opportunities for reassortment among otherwise geographically separated strains. Despite substantial genetic diversity and reassortment, all viruses remained antigenically similar based on haemagglutination inhibition and virus neutralisation assays. However, a representative strain from one subgroup induced significantly lower homologous and heterologous antibody titres, suggesting reduced immunogenicity. Our findings demonstrate a notable disconnect between genetic evolution and antigenic change in Bangladeshi H9N2 viruses. While reassortment and genetic diversification continue to shape viral populations, antigenic properties remain largely conserved, supporting the continued relevance of current vaccine strategies while highlighting the importance of ongoing genetic and antigenic surveillance.

papers.title: Liver Immunity-Guided Discovery of Capsule-Permeable Protein Antigens Against Bacterial Sepsis
papers.abstract: The capsules of invasive bacteria shield underlying antigens, limit immune clearance and hinder vaccine noncapsular antigen discovery. To address this, we developed Liver-based Vaccine Antigen Capture (L-VAC), a functional platform integrating antibody-mediated screening with in vivo visualization of hepatic bacterial clearance in mice. Applying L-VAC to Streptococcus pneumoniae identified multiple capsule-permeable proteins that induce rapid hepatic clearance of blood-borne bacteria. Immunization with these proteins, especially in a multivalent formulation, conferred broad cross-serotype protection. Spatial analyses revealed that only the proteins localized at or near the capsular surface are targetable for vaccine-induced pathogen capture in the liver sinusoids. These findings establish L-VAC as a sensitive and reliable approach for identifying protective protein antigens capable of overcoming capsule barriers, offering a promising strategy to develop broadly protective vaccines against multidrug-resistant encapsulated pathogens.

papers.title: Multi-locus pairing expands the functional repertoire of two-peptide bacteriocins
papers.abstract: Two-peptide bacteriocins are generally viewed as self-contained systems whose peptides are encoded at the same biosynthetic locus and co-expressed to form an active antimicrobial pair. Here, we show that functional pairing extends beyond this organization. Comparative genomic analysis revealed frequent co-occurrence of putative two-peptide bacteriocins encoded at distinct chromosomal loci in streptococci. Testing pairwise combinations of 47 peptides produced by cell-free protein synthesis identified 54 combinations with enhanced antimicrobial activity, with inter-locus combinations more frequent than intra-locus combinations. In Streptococcus mitis strain C22, four dispersed bacteriocin loci are coordinately expressed during exponential growth despite regulation by partially independent signaling pathways, providing an opportunity for inter-locus pairing. Split-luciferase complementation assays showed that active peptide pairs associate and that these interactions depend predominantly on amino acid sequence. Using a bacteriocin-free S. mitis background, we further show that components produced by distinct bacterial cells can act together to increase producer competitiveness in co-culture with S. pneumoniae. These findings reveal a modular organization in which peptides encoded at different loci can form functional combinations, including when produced by separate cells. This flexibility expands the antimicrobial repertoire available to individual strains and provides a mechanism for bacteriocin diversification while retaining functional compatibility.

papers.title: The FraA adhesin and Ebp pili mediate Enterococcus faecalis adhesion under fluid flow
papers.abstract: Enterococcus faecalis is a frequent cause of infective endocarditis and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI). Successful colonization is challenged by blood and urine flow and relies on a strong and resilient bacterial attachment. Here, we identify molecular determinants that enable E. faecalis to maintain adhesion under flow, notably the flow-related adhesin (FraA), a previously uncharacterized adhesion factor encoded by OG1RF_11764. Transcriptomic analysis revealed increased fraA expression in surface-attached bacteria exposed to shear stress. Structural predictions identified an N-terminal region with homology to characterized Gram-positive adhesins, followed by tandem CLIPPER repeats with putative isopeptide-bond-forming residues and a C-terminal cell-wall sorting signal. Using microfluidics and single-cell tracking, we found that deletion of fraA accelerated detachment from hydrophobic abiotic surfaces under fluid flow. In line with this finding, loss of fraA reduced catheter colonization in a murine CAUTI model. Analysis of 9,192 E. faecalis genomes identified FraA in 50.8% of isolates, spanning clinical and non-clinical sources, with sequence type-associated variation in CLIPPER repeat number. Another determinant, Ebp pilus, enhances adhesion at high shear stress and contributes to a shear-enhanced adhesion pattern. Collectively, these findings identify FraA as an adhesion factor contributing to medical-device colonization and together with Ebp pili support attachment across different hydrodynamic conditions. Identifying these adhesion mechanisms could inform strategies to prevent colonization of medical devices exposed to fluid flow.

papers.title: Mechanical unloading and exercise volume differentially modulate the gut microbiome and intestinal gene expression in mice
papers.abstract: Mechanical unloading and physical activity can influence the gut microbiome and intestinal physiology, but the effects of exercise volume and prior hindlimb suspension remain incompletely understood. This study investigated how hindlimb suspension, different exercise volumes, and exercise following hindlimb suspension affect gut microbial composition and intestinal gene expression in mice. Mice were assigned to five groups: control (C), hindlimb suspension (HL), high-volume exercise (HE), low-volume exercise (LE), and hindlimb suspension followed by exercise (HLE). Cecal microbiota composition was characterized using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, followed by alpha- and beta-diversity analyses and LinDA differential-abundance analysis. Jejunal gene expression was assessed by quantitative PCR for markers related to oxidative stress, inflammation, metabolic signaling, and epithelial function. Hindlimb suspension reduced microbial richness, as indicated by the Observed, Chao1, and ACE indices, and was associated with a significant difference in overall microbial community composition compared with controls. It was also associated with reductions in Streptococcaceae/Streptococcus and Spirochaetota. Low-volume exercise produced the most extensive phylum-level differential-abundance findings, whereas high-volume exercise showed no significant phylum-level differences from controls. Both exercise groups (HE and LE) exhibited increased intestinal expression of GPX1, HMOX1, NFKB1, and SOD2. HE also increased IGF and MUC2 expression, whereas HLE reduced IGF expression compared with controls. Community composition did not differ significantly between HLE and HL, and LGR5 expression did not differ significantly among groups. In conclusion, hindlimb suspension was associated with reduced microbial richness and selective taxonomic changes, whereas low-volume exercise produced the most extensive phylum-level alterations in microbial composition. Exercise volume was also associated with distinct intestinal transcriptional responses, while exercise following mechanical unloading did not produce a microbial community composition significantly different from that observed following unloading alone. These findings highlight the context-dependent effects of mechanical unloading and exercise on gut microbial composition and intestinal gene expression.

papers.title: Characterization of anaerobic bacterial populations putatively involved in the degradation of Chlorine pesticides in mangrove soils of Guadeloupe (Lesser Antilles).
papers.abstract: Due to their position at the land-sea interface and their proximity to contaminated agricultural areas, mangroves are ecosystems potentially exposed to chlordecone pollution. This study aims to describe, for the first time, the composition of bacterial communities in mangrove soils and their distribution according to chlordecone contamination. The results revealed marked inter-site heterogeneity in bacterial communities across the three study sites, encompassing both an uncontaminated mangrove (Manche &agrave eau; chlordecone concentrations below the detection limit, <5 g kg-1) and contaminated mangroves (Sarcelle and Petite rivi&egravere de Goyave), where soil chlordecone concentrations ranged from <5 to 118.8 g kg-1 along the coastal-to-agricultural transects. Between 60 and 90% of the detected taxa belong to groups involved in the degradation of aromatic compounds, while 5 to 15% correspond to genera associated with nitrification processes. This diversity does not appear to be directly correlated with the presence of chlordecone, suggesting the predominant influence of other environmental factors. Nevertheless, two bacterial genera of interest were identified, Dehalogenimonas and Desulfomonile, known for their involvement in the degradation of aromatic compounds according to the FAPROTAX analysis. Furthermore, functional analysis based on the KEGG database suggests the presence of vitamin B12 biosynthesis pathways in Dehalogenimonas and Desulfomonile (found in coastal areas), as well as in Burkholderia (found in agricultural soils). These results suggest the existence of metabolic potential to intervene in both the chemical and biological processes of chlordecone degradation. Finally, mangroves appear to have purification potential favorable to chlordecone degradation, due to the presence of Dehalogenimonas and several other bacterial genera capable of participating in the chemical and/or biological degradation processes of chlordecone.

papers.title: The infectious unit of influenza A virus is a population of particles, not a single virion, as shown by absolute particle quantification
papers.abstract: Influenza A virus (IAV) populations are characterized by a high prevalence of non-infectious virions, with particle-to-plaque forming unit (PFU) ratios typically ranging from 10 to 1,000. While "multiplicity reactivation" -the process by which incomplete viral genomes (IVGs) establish productive infection through co-infection- has long been hypothesized, its quantitative nature has remained elusive. In this study, we utilized a digital influenza assay to achieve absolute quantification of IAV particles, allowing us to define the particle-based multiplicity of infection (pMOI) for precise evaluation. We combined this approach with a single-cell infection assay using microcompartmentalized containers and machine learning-based automated cell classification to accurately assess infection outcomes across a wide range of pMOIs. Our analysis of the A/Puerto Rico/8/1934 (H1N1) revealed a count-to-plaque forming unit (PFU) ratio of approximately 400, meaning only a tiny fraction of particles possesses infectivity. Remarkably, the infection rate in single-cell infection experiments followed a sigmoidal curve and reached saturation at a pMOI of only 5 to 10. This demonstrates that under high-pMOI conditions, productive infection is predominantly driven by genome complementation among incomplete particles rather than solely by fully infectious virions. On the other hand, mathematical model analysis based on these findings suggested that the functionality of each of the eight genomic segments within a virus particle follows a stochastic process, resulting in a probability distribution for the number of functional segments per particle. This mechanism proved exceptionally robust across multiple strains despite a 20-fold variation in CTPR values. Ultimately, these findings indicate that incomplete particles are not merely biological noise but active contributors to the infection process, significantly enhancing the infectivity and evolutionary flexibility of IAV. This study will provide a more refined understanding of influenza transmission dynamics and risk assessment, particularly in environments where multiple virus particles are present within a single respiratory droplet.

papers.title: A conserved tyrosine in the S1/S2 loop shapes SARS-CoV-2 spike processing and host protease usage.
papers.abstract: Both spike processing efficiency and host protease usage play critical roles in SARS-CoV-2 infection, pathogenesis, and transmission. The SARS-CoV-2 spike contains two motifs, a furin cleavage site (FCS) and an extended S1/S2 loop, which improve both cleavage efficiency and host protease usage. Disruption of these motifs significantly attenuates SARS-CoV-2 infection and pathogenesis. Importantly, modifications and changes within the S1/S2 loop can also shape infection and disease outcomes following infection. In this study, we examined mass spectrometry data generated from purified virions from wild-type (WT) or mutant SARS-CoV-2 infection. We identified phosphorylation occurring at highly conserved residue Y674 and used reverse genetics to generate a mutant that ablates phosphorylation capacity in the S1/ S2 loop (Y674F). Our results show that the Y674F mutant replicated equivalently to wild-type SARS-CoV-2 in Vero cells but had attenuated replication in a human respiratory cell line. Golden Syrian hamsters infected with the Y674F mutant had equivalent weight loss, lung viral titer, and similar immune pathology to WT SARS-CoV-2. However, the mutant had reduced viral load in the nasal wash and reduced antigen staining in the large airways in the lung. Notably, loss of Y674 ablated spike processing to the S1/S2 cleavage product on virions. In addition, Y674F mutant had a diminished capacity to utilize host protease TMPRSS2 for entry. Together, these data indicates that post-translational modification of Y674 impacts SARS-CoV-2 infection of the airway by disrupting both spike processing and host protease function. These results add to data demonstrating the importance of spike S1/S2 loop modifications to SARS-CoV-2 infection, pathogenesis, and transmission.

papers.title: Phage peptide promotes bacterial cell death via inner and outer membrane targets
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) play a major role in mammalian innate immunity by preferentially targeting bacterial membranes through charge-dependent interactions. While CAMPs are extensively studied in eukaryotic systems, less is known about phage-encoded CAMPs and their role in bacterial lysis. Here, we characterize gp28, a 56-aa cationic peptide encoded by the T7-like coliphage phiKT to define its mechanism of membrane disruption and bacteriostatic activity. Biochemical fractionation reveals that gp28 is asymmetrically distributed across bacterial membranes. Supporting its direct role in causing cell death, gp28 induces permeability changes at the inner membrane. Using synthetic gp28 peptide, we also show that gp28 activity is blocked by lipopolysaccharide and divalent cation competition. This led us to discover that gp28 is also active against Gram-positive bacteria in a surface charge-dependent manner. Finally, we demonstrate gp28 has broad bacteriostatic activity against multiple Gram-negative species, including clinical Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) isolates. Together, our results support a model in which gp28 exploits charge-based interactions with bacterial surface molecules to gain access to membranes, then destabilizes the envelope to promote host cell death. These findings expand our understanding of phage lysis strategies and highlight phage-derived peptides as potential scaffolds for antimicrobial development. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Cationic antimicrobial peptides produced by eukaryotes target and disrupt bacterial membranes. These peptides are integral members of the innate immune system and potential antibacterials. Due to their cellular origin, the genetics to understand their mechanisms of action are cumbersome. Here, we demonstrate functional similarity between a bacteriophage peptide called gp28 and cationic antimicrobial peptides. Gp28 partitions between both membranes of Gram-negative bacteria and reduces their integrity. We show that gp28 employs charge-based interactions to associate with and disrupt membranes, suggesting that gp28 targets charged polymers on the membrane surface. Additionally, gp28 inhibits the growth of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, and renders them more susceptible to antibiotics. Our studies provide a foundation for future genetics and development of phage peptide-based antimicrobials.

papers.title: Multi-specific nanobody-Fc fusions against TcdB protect in vivo from diverse Clostridioides difficile strains
papers.abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is an urgent antibiotic-associated threat and the leading cause of nosocomial diarrhea in the United States, with a high rate of recurrence. Antibiotics are the standard of care for treating CDI but can prolong microbial dysbiosis in the gut. The only FDA-approved monoclonal antibody (mAb) for the prevention of recurrent CDI, Zinplava (bezlotoxumab), was discontinued in January 2025. The target of bezlotoxumab is the dominant virulence factor of C. difficile, the exotoxin B (TcdB). However, TcdB sequences vary across strains and encompass twelve distinct subtypes. Consequently, sequence variation between subtypes presents a challenge for the identification of pan-neutralizing mAb therapeutics. Here, we describe the generation of three bi-specific and one tri-specific nanobody-Fc fusions targeting TcdB. Each fusion neutralizes TcdB in vitro across clinically relevant subtypes with greater potency than bezlotoxumab. In a mouse model of CDI, using three diverse C. difficile strains, several of the fusion proteins improve infection outcomes over bezlotoxumab when administered prophylactically. We also highlight one fusion that improves survival in a therapeutic mouse model of CDI. These data demonstrate multi-specific nanobody-Fc fusions as a strategy to improve potency and mitigate the impact of sequence variation within the toxin. Our fusions outperform the standards established by bezlotoxumab and represent strong candidates for translation.

papers.title: bofasa enables high-quality orthology inference across diverse multi-species bacterial genome sets
papers.abstract: Bacterial species can be separated by billions of years of evolution. However, studies of such ancient relationships often rely on methods developed for eukaryotes, which are less diverse. Such methods can regard instances of horizontal gene transfer as contamination, rely heavily on a species phylogeny when partitioning paralogs, and fail to account for the multi-domain architectures of some genes. Here, we introduce, showcase, and benchmark bofasa, a software for high-quality and automated inference of ortholog groups across distantly related bacterial species. bofasa employs a recursive algorithm to split coarse homolog groups into paralogous subsets and first establishes domain-level ortholog groups prior to assessing evolutionary relationships between entire proteins. In comparison to other methods commonly used for multi-species bacterial comparative genomics, bofasa is substantially more conservative in predicting orthology yet can often recover the largest single-copy core genome. Beyond orthology inference, the software also features several additional utility functionalities, including assessment of which ortholog groups are commonly found on mobile genetic elements or possess variable genomic contexts.

papers.title: Exploring taxonomic diversity in the genus Suberites Nardo, 1833: Insights from microbial, phylogenetic, and morphological analyses
papers.abstract: Marine sponges (phylum Porifera) are a highly diverse and polymorphic group of marine invertebrates whose taxonomic delimitation is often challenging due to high intraspecific variability and the scarcity of diagnostic morphological characters. Their close association with microbial symbionts also makes them an important source of secondary metabolites, some of which may contribute to sponge colouration. Here, we use morphological characters, molecular phylogenetic markers, and 16S metabarcoding of the symbiont community to understand speciation in a common Mediterranean sponge lineage. We collected 43 specimens of the genus Suberites from the Mediterranean Sea and the North and South Atlantic Oceans, between 55-150 m depths, and sequenced two barcoding genes, cytochrome c oxidase I and 28S rDNA, as well as studied their spicular complements. We identified five closely-related species: S. domuncula, S. ficus/pagurorum, S. dandelenae, S. ambulodomus, and a new species of Suberites from the Balearic Islands, Suberites sp. nov. The latter represents a potential new pseudo-cryptic species closely related to S. domuncula, because of their strong morphological and molecular affinities. The potential new Mediterranean species exhibits six colour morphotypes (yellow, gray, orange, brown, red, and blue), and the microbiome analyses of the symbiotic communities revealed significant differences in bacterial community composition among colour morphotypes, specially of bacteria that produce different pigments which potentially give the sponge is colouration. These results provide valuable insights into species boundaries and evolutionary relationships within the genus Suberites and support a role for the microbiome in sponge colouration.

papers.title: RAMP-Seq: a single-tube nanopore workflow for co-amplifying full-length 16S rRNA and antimicrobial resistance genes for integrated taxonomic and resistance profiling
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance needs workflows that both identify bacteria and detect resistance genes from a single sample, but current targeted nanopore assays typically split these steps into separate reactions or library preparations. We introduce RAMP-Seq (Rapid AMR Profiling by Sequencing), a workflow that simultaneously amplifies the full-length 16S rRNA gene (~1,500 bp) together with eight resistance determinants (~600 - 700 bp) in a single multiplex PCR and then sequences the resulting mixed-length amplicon pool as a single nanopore library. The eight-primer pair set targets dominant alleles of {beta}-lactamase, carbapenemase, quinolone-resistance and silver-resistance families. Read-length distributions confirmed that both size classes were co-amplified evenly using a single, non-equimolar primer pool. From extracted DNA to the first taxonomically classified reads took 8.2 {+/-} 0.6 h. Full-length 16S sequencing of an eight-member mock community identified all anticipated taxa, and the observed abundances closely followed the expected log-scaled composition (Pearson's r = 0.879). The full nineplex amplicon assay was subsequently tested on three distinct matrices: pooled clinical isolates, spiked human blood, and environmental water samples. Using an equal-mass pool of genomic DNA from eleven multidrug-resistant clinical and repository isolates, the full assay produced genus-level and resistance-gene profiles that were consistent across biological replicates (r = 0.998 and r = 0.824), and it specifically identified all seven panel targets present, confirmed by Illumina whole-genome sequencing. After carbonate-based host DNA depletion, Klebsiella pneumoniae was recovered from spiked human blood at every titration down to 102 CFU/mL, as were all five panel targets carried by that strain. Across five water-sampling sites from a sewage treatment plant (STP) to a connected lake system, microbial communities and resistance-gene profiles were site-specific: influent and effluent communities overlapped little, while the lake inlet and outlet were similar. Target resistance genes were most numerous and abundant in STP influent, fewer in effluent, and rare or absent in lake and well samples. Because bacterial identification relies on amplification of the conserved, near-universal 16S rRNA gene, rather than on species-specific primer sets, RAMP-Seq can detect and taxonomically classify bacteria in a design-agnostic manner. The same single-tube chemistry therefore serves sample types as different as clinical specimens and environmental water and is extendable to longer ribosomal targets and further resistance-gene families.

papers.title: Development of African Swine Fever Virus Pseudotype Systems for Ba71v and Georgia 2007 strains
papers.abstract: African swine fever virus (ASFV) is a large, complex DNA virus that causes a severe haemorrhagic disease in domestic swine and Eurasian wild boar. Due to its high pathogenicity, research involving ASFV is restricted to high-containment laboratories, which significantly limits investigations into its biology, host interactions and the development of effective control measures. To overcome these limitations, this study utilised pseudotyped virus (PV) technology to identify ASFV proteins involved in cell entry. Candidate proteins were identified through bioinformatic analysis and a review of the published literature, incorporated into PVs, and subsequently assessed for their ability to facilitate cellular entry. This approach identified a combination of three ASFV proteins that, when combined, resulted in the most efficient cell entry. This work represents the successful generation of the first functional ASF pseudotype system for both Ba71v and Georgia 2007 strains, enabling the safe study of ASFV entry mechanisms under containment level 2.

papers.title: A polarized genome is required for fitness of the obligate intracellular, tick-borne pathogen Rickettsia parkeri
papers.abstract: Alphaproteobacteria of the order Rickettsiales include biomedically important, yet understudied arthropod-borne human pathogens. These pathogens lack obvious morphological asymmetry, but encode homologs of key mediators of polar processes in the model Alphaproteobacterium Caulobacter crescentus. These include the polar organizing protein PopZ, the chromosome segregation proteins ParA and ParB, and the spatial regulator of cell division MipZ. Motivated by this observation, we used the tick-borne human pathogen Rickettsia parkeri to ask if the chromosome is polarized and coordinated with cell division in this group. Consistent with that hypothesis, we found that transposon insertion mutants in parA, parB, mipZ, or popZ resulted in cell division defects. Fluorescence imaging revealed cell cycle-dependent unipolar-to-bipolar localization dynamics of ParB and MipZ, and pole-to-midcell dynamics of the division protein ZapA. This patterning parallels the model of chromosome segregation and cell division site selection established in Caulobacter. Unlike its unipolar-to-bipolar dynamics in Caulobacter, however, PopZ remained at a single cell pole throughout the cell cycle in R. parkeri. PopZ maintained its direct interaction with ParA and ParB. Interestingly, disruption of parA or parB, but not popZ or mipZ, caused a small plaque phenotype, suggesting a defect in growth or spread in a monolayer of host cells in the absence of proper chromosome segregation. We propose that genome polarization in R. parkeri and other rickettsiae is critical both for fundamental cellular processes and for interactions with host cells that promote fitness in their infectious niche.
